# 1. Introduction

Financial inclusion, understood as access to and use of savings, credit, payment and insurance services, is a standard instrument of development policy, and the case for it is pressed hardest in economies whose output and employment rest on smallholder agriculture. Account ownership among adults in developing economies has widened substantially over the past decade, but unevenly, and rural and farming households remain among the least served [@DemirgucKunt2017; @Klapper2025]. In sub-Saharan Africa the shortfall is largest, inclusion tracks income, schooling, age and gender most sharply [@Zins2016], and the recent widening has come through mobile money rather than through banks [@Aker2010; @WorldBank2024]. It is also where meta-analytic evidence on African agriculture finds farms operating persistently below best practice, with access to inputs and improved technology among the recurring explanations [@Ogundari2014]. Ghana sits squarely in this pattern: the two rounds of the Ghana Living Standards Survey (GLSS) used here record the same widening among rural households and a shift in the institutions through which they save and borrow [@GSS2014; @GSS2019].

The economic case for extending these services to farmers rests on the liquidity constraint. Smallholders face lumpy, seasonally concentrated outlays on planting material, fertilizer, agro-chemicals and hired labour months before harvest income arrives, and households that cannot borrow against the harvest under-apply inputs, mis-time them or forgo technologies whose fixed costs they cannot pre-finance [@Guirkinger2008; @Kumar2013; @Dercon2011]. Credit that relaxes this constraint should, in principle, let farms adopt the practices of the best-performing producers and operate nearer to the best-practice production frontier, with the gains for productivity and food security that a large efficiency literature on African agriculture anticipates [@Ogundari2014; @Meyer2015].

Whether it does so in practice depends on which margin of farm performance one examines, and the two margins call for different policy responses. Output differences among farmers arise from two distinct sources: some farmers operate a less productive technology set than the best-performing group, and some use whatever technology they have less efficiently. The meta-stochastic frontier (MSF) framework separates these margins by benchmarking group-specific frontiers against a common metafrontier, so that the technology gap ratio (TGR) captures the productive capacity of a group's technology relative to best practice, technical efficiency (TE) captures how well its members exploit it, and their product, meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE), measures overall performance against best practice. If credit users differ from non-users mainly in the technology they operate, the relevant instruments concern input systems, mechanization services and the terms on which a loan can be turned into farm investment; if they differ mainly in efficiency, the constraints lie in management, information and the timing of input use. A single production frontier estimated over both groups cannot tell these apart, because it forces both onto one technology and attributes every difference to inefficiency. Applications of the framework to Ghanaian crop production show that the two margins are empirically separable and that their relative weight varies across ecologies, crops, operator gender and age [@Ansah2023a; @Tsiboe2021a; @Adaku2023; @Asravor2024]; the same decomposition has been applied to variety adoption in Ghana [@AbdulRahaman2021] and to credit access among cocoa farmers in Nigeria [@Awotide2015], but not, to our knowledge, to credit use in a nationally representative sample of Ghanaian farms.

The Ghanaian evidence on credit and farm performance is instead largely crop-specific, regional and cross-sectional, and it points in different directions. The one experimental exception is also the closest counterpart to the question asked here: randomizing capital grants and rainfall-index insurance among maize farmers in northern Ghana, @Karlan2014 find that farm investment responded to the relaxation of risk rather than of liquidity, a design that establishes which constraint binds — something the observational comparison drawn here cannot do — for one crop in one region and for credit that is offered rather than sought. Elsewhere the record is observational. Participation in input-credit schemes in northern Ghana raised fertilizer and labour use among maize farmers with only modest output gains and no detectable income effect [@Iddrisu2018]; bank-linked credit did not raise the technical efficiency of smallholder rice producers relative to non-borrowers [@Anang2016]; formal and informal financing arrangements were associated with higher technical or economic efficiency among maize producers [@Martey2019; @AppiahTwumasi2019; @AppiahTwumasi2022]; and a broader indicator of financial inclusion has been linked to smallholder productivity [@Peprah2021]. Two features of that observational literature limit what can be concluded from it. First, each study estimates a single frontier for borrowers and non-borrowers, so an efficiency difference may be a technology difference in disguise. Second, borrowers are not a random draw of farmers, and comparisons that do not first balance who borrows against who does not conflate the correlates of borrowing with any association of borrowing itself. Two further features of rural credit complicate the interpretation of any credit contrast. Loans are fungible, so a loan recorded against a farm household need not reach the farm [@Hussain2016], and the population that uses credit differs from the population that has access to it, since demand-side constraints can bind as tightly as supply-side ones [@DeJanvry2020].

Ghana between 2012/13 and 2016/17 is a useful setting in which to ask the question in these terms, because inclusion widened on some margins and not on others. Among the crop farmers studied here, formal account ownership rose from `r tbl_pct("table2", "Has bank account/contributing to a scheme (binary)", 1, 1)` to `r tbl_pct("table2", "Has bank account/contributing to a scheme (binary)", 2, 1)` between the two rounds, yet the share of operators who applied for a loan stayed below one in ten (`r tbl_pct("table3", "Loan applied", 1, 1)` and `r tbl_pct("table3", "Loan applied", 2, 1)`), the modal reason for not applying was that no loan was needed, lending shifted toward group-based schemes, and in 2012/13 only `r tbl_pct("table3", "Agricultural", 1, 1)` of the loans held by farm households were reported as taken for agricultural purposes (Section 3). The households that borrow are therefore a small group whose loans are, for the most part, not farm loans, and any account of what credit does for crop production has to be consistent with that record.

This paper asks three questions. First, do farm households that use credit operate a different crop production technology from comparable households that do not, as reflected in input elasticities and returns to scale? Second, where their performance differs, does the difference arise from the technology set they operate (TGR), from the efficiency with which they operate it (TE), or from both? Third, do these associations depend on which household member holds the loan, on the other financial services the household uses, and on operator gender, age and education, crop and region?

To answer them we pool the farmer-level records of GLSS waves 6 (2012/13) and 7 (2016/17), the two rounds that administer the credit and financial-services module in comparable form, and reconstruct credit use from the original questionnaires. The sample, drawn from a nationally representative survey, comprises `r fmt_num(objs$sample$n_pooled, 0)` crop farm operators, of whom `r fmt_pct(objs$treatment$share_treated, 1)` live in a household in which the operator, a spouse, a child or another member applied for a loan in the preceding twelve months, was granted it and recorded a positive amount; this household-level indicator is the preferred treatment because liquidity is pooled within the farm household. We estimate separate translog stochastic frontiers for credit-using and non-using households, envelop them with a stochastic metafrontier, and form the comparison on a sample in which each credit user is paired one-to-one with a non-user matched exactly on survey wave, region, agro-ecological zone, locality type and operator gender and closely on demographic, household, cropping and financial-inclusion characteristics [@Abadie2006; @Abadie2016; @Stuart2010], following a small literature that combines the metafrontier with matching where the technology group is self-selected [@Mayen2010; @BravoUreta2021; @Asmare2022]. Standard errors for every quantity, including each group difference, come from a cluster jackknife over enumeration areas that re-runs matching and estimation in every replicate. Because the GLSS records credit use rather than credit access, offers no credible instrument for household borrowing, and cannot balance unobserved determinants of borrowing such as managerial ability, risk preference or standing with lenders, we interpret every difference reported here as an association conditional on observables in a balanced sample, not as a causal effect of credit; Section 4 sets out what that interpretation permits.

The results do not conform to the liquidity-constraint story that motivates the expansion of rural credit. Credit users' group frontier does differ from non-users', with a markedly larger family-labour elasticity and higher returns to scale, but relative to the common best-practice frontier, credit-using households operate a less productive technology set, not a more productive one. In the matched sample their technology gap ratio averages `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 3, block = "Technology gap ratio (TGR)"), 3)` against `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 2, block = "Technology gap ratio (TGR)"), 3)` for matched non-users, a shortfall of `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 4, block = "Technology gap ratio (TGR)")), 1)` percentage points that keeps its sign under every definition of who in the household holds the loan, under alternative matching distances, functional forms, efficiency estimators and aggregation rules, among account holders and non-holders alike, and in nearly every gender, age, education, crop and regional subgroup, cocoa producers being the one clear exception. The technical-efficiency difference within groups is small by comparison and its sign is not stable across specifications, so the lower meta-frontier efficiency of credit users, a shortfall of between `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 4, block = "Meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE)")), 1)` and `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table5", "Anyone including farmer", 3, block = "Meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE)")), 1)` percentage points depending on the specification, is a technology gap rather than a management gap. Balancing the two groups on observables removes most of the raw efficiency disadvantage of borrowers but little of the technology gap, and matched credit users apply less fertilizer, planting material, hired labour and pesticide per hectare than their comparators without a significantly different value of output per hectare. Section 5 weighs the readings the data can speak to: that borrowing households are not, as a group, the ones operating the best-practice technology; that most household credit finances activity off the farm; that selection into borrowing on characteristics the survey does not record cannot be excluded; and that the comparison is between users and non-users rather than between the constrained and the unconstrained.

The paper makes three contributions. First, it provides, to our knowledge, the first nationally representative evidence for Ghana that decomposes the performance difference between credit-using and non-using farm households into a technology margin and an efficiency margin, so that a lower technology gap ratio and an unchanged technical efficiency can be told apart; the existing evidence, confined to single crops, regions and frontiers, cannot make that distinction. Second, it measures credit at the household level, reports how the contrast changes when the borrower is the operator, the spouse or another member, and combines the metafrontier with matching and a full-pipeline jackknife, so that the borrower/non-borrower contrast is drawn between observably comparable households and carries the uncertainty of the pairing as well as of the estimation. Third, it reconstructs the financial-services modules of the GLSS to document the state of financial inclusion among crop farmers and uses that detail to examine whether the credit association differs among households that are otherwise financially included, and across operator, crop and regional subgroups, which is the information a policy that bundles credit with payment, advisory or risk services would need [@Barrett2022; @Meyer2015]. The finding that borrowing households operate a technology farther inside the national frontier than comparable non-borrowers reframes the policy question from how much credit reaches farm households to what the credit they already obtain is buying.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the data, the construction of the credit and financial-service indicators from the GLSS questionnaires, and the descriptive statistics of credit users and non-users. Section 3 documents the state of financial inclusion and credit access among Ghanaian crop farmers over the two rounds and draws out what it implies for the design. Section 4 states the hypotheses, presents the meta-stochastic frontier specification and the matching design, delimits what the design identifies, and describes inference and the robustness programme. Section 5 reports diagnostics, output elasticities, the technology and efficiency decomposition, its interpretation, robustness checks and heterogeneity, with discussion integrated. Section 6 concludes with the implications for policy and research.
